messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rajesh, a 41-year-old South Asian man married with two children, works as a graphic designer and has been struggling to cope since his traumatic encounter with police nearly a year ago. The event occurred one evening when he was returning home from work. A routine traffic stop escalated rapidly into an aggressive confrontation, leaving Rajesh feeling vulnerable and betrayed by the very figures meant to protect him. Since then, any burnt smell—a common detail during confrontations—triggers intense flashbacks for Rajesh. Whenever he encounters a person in uniform, even on television or at a distance, his heart races and he feels as though he is reliving that harrowing experience. Each time he recalls the event, it evokes a profound sense of guilt, as if somehow he could have prevented what happened. Rajesh has come to believe that the world is a dangerous place and that people cannot be trusted. These beliefs have made him hypervigilant, constantly scanning for potential threats. When Rajesh sees someone in uniform or smells burnt items, his mind replays the traumatic scene, making it difficult for him to find words to describe what happened and leaving him unable to explain clearly when he attempts to share. His negative appraisals reinforce each other: because he feels betrayed by those he trusted, he is more vigilant of authority figures. This cycle leaves Rajesh feeling constantly on edge, as if the world around him is a threat at every turn. He has begun rehearsing conversations in advance and avoids making any future plans, fearing that something similar might happen again. Rajesh’s hypervigilance extends to his work environment. One day while working late at his office, a janitor wearing a uniform passed by the door of Rajesh's workspace, triggering an immediate surge of anxiety. He felt as though he was back on the street with police, and his heart pounded in his chest. This incident led him to avoid social gatherings or any events where authority figures might be present. His inability to articulate what happened has further compounded his distress. When trying to explain it to his wife, Rajesh loses track of his thoughts and ends up feeling frustrated and misunderstood. His maladaptive strategies have only deepened the issue; he is convinced that by rehearsing conversations and avoiding future plans, he can mitigate the risk of a similar event occurring again. Rajesh's world has become smaller as he has isolated himself from social activities and even some work functions where he might encounter people in uniform. He feels increasingly trapped by his fears and is now seeking help because he realizes that these strategies are no longer working. What frightens him most is the possibility of another traumatic event, but what gives him hope is finding a way to regain control over his life without the constant fear. Rajesh's journey toward therapy has been motivated by the desire to reclaim his sense of safety and trust in the world around him, as well as the hope that he can once again enjoy simple moments without being overwhelmed by triggers or hypervigilance.
